fields.title: Unequal Power Was Not Unequal Worth
fields.content:
Colonial society included unequal power and privileges. A privilege is an advantage given to particular people or groups. Historical records could use categories connected with ancestry, birthplace, office or tax status. These categories were made and used within a system of rule. They were not a measure of intelligence, character or human worth.

In this mission, we examine what a label did in a particular record. Did it affect a payment, an office or access to an opportunity? Do not treat every category as one fixed ladder applying unchanged to all people throughout Spanish rule. A person could have several roles, and social relationships could change. Our fictional record cards are tools for asking questions, not a game of assigning classmates to ranks. Students will not disclose ancestry or receive points for belonging to a group.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit this lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: An Office and a Person Were Different
fields.content:
Local elites could connect colonial authorities with community affairs. Majuls discussion describes the principalia in relation to town offices and families. Knowing that a person held office helps identify a role, but not every action that person took. A title does not prove fair conduct, universal approval or identical behavior by all officeholders.

Compare fictional cards for an instruction, an officeholder and a complaint. The instruction concerns an official task. The name identifies a person in a role. The complaint records a reported problem. Connect them only when their people, place and period match. Do not assume that local leaders always agreed with every colonial demand or that every official had the same resources. A local role could involve carrying out instructions and raising difficulties; each action needs its own evidence.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit this lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: Labels Could Shape Treatment
fields.content:
Colonial labels could affect treatment in matters such as taxation and local authority. Aguilars study of Gregorio Sancianco explains a critique of tribute as a source of divisions among people. This connects a revenue system with social relationships. A category in a record is therefore something to investigate, not a neutral description of every part of a persons life.

Use a fictional tax register with two category headings but no rates supplied. The headings show that the writer distinguished groups. They do not let us invent exact payment amounts or conclude that every member had the same wealth, work or opportunities. To explain an actual difference, find the dated rule and the relevant entry. We may discuss the historical term mestizo when a source uses it, but it does not automatically mean wealthy, official or one identical background in every record.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit this lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: Compare Opportunities in Everyday Life
fields.content:
Unequal resources and power could shape everyday opportunities. Access to schooling, time for work, control of resources and connections with officials are questions to investigate. A category alone cannot tell us exactly how every household experienced them. Records about an institution or a prominent person may leave other people less visible.

Compare two fictional learner cards without ancestry labels. One has time, materials and a nearby class; the other lacks those supports. The model shows why an available opportunity on paper is not necessarily equally reachable. It is not a historical census or a claim about every child in one group. Ask what support and constraints each card describes. We do not ask students to disclose family income or judge classmates. For a historical report, replace assumptions with dated evidence about particular people and circumstances.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit this lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: A Named Case: A Petition from Bacolor
fields.content:
A UP Diliman research summary describes Chinese mestizo chiefs in Bacolor, Pampanga, petitioning colonial authorities in 1698 for relief from tribute-collection duties. The case connects a social category with a local role and a request. It shows why a label alone is too small to explain a persons place in community life.

The study discusses an investigation and local relationships, including recognition by native elites. This is a particular historical case, not a rule that every petition succeeded or every person in the category held land. Separate the request, the investigation and any documented result. Our labelled clue card is a modern source guide, not a surviving petition page. We do not invent speeches, signatures or personal motives. Explain what people requested and what evidence the study provides, while leaving wider claims open to further investigation.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit this lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.

fields.title: Prepare Your Everyday Experience Report
fields.content:
Review five ideas. Hierarchies involved unequal power and privilege, not unequal human worth. An office identified a role rather than every action. Categories could affect treatment without explaining a whole life. Practical conditions shaped opportunities. The Bacolor petition is a named case connecting categories, roles and a recorded request.

Prepare a fictional report for another Grade 5 learner. Name the people or role, place and period. Give a supporting clue and identify what you cannot yet know. Do not turn a category into guaranteed wealth, intelligence or behavior. Label learner cards as fictional models, and separate a petition from its documented outcome. You do not need to disclose ancestry, religion or family finances.

The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. If needed, return to linked learning content before practice and a retry. Completing this mission earns its configured reward once, but does not complete Chapter 10. Missions 4-5 and the chapter challenge are still being prepared.
